seo.title: Karmic tail 12 16 4 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 16 4 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Emperor — a pause instead of plain words, a day of truth and a house law written by two.

title: The couple's karmic tail 12-16-4: The Hanged Man, The Tower and The Emperor
short: The Hebrew Bible contains a book in which the name of God never appears, and its heroine bears a name that is read both as "she who hides" and as "star". It is the Book of Esther, and its plot shows through the karmic tail 12-16-4 in compatibility in the same order as the cards: the couple enters its task through a pause and things left unsaid, passes through a day when everything hidden comes out at once, and its main task is the law of its own house.

sections.h2: A book that opens with a decree about marriage
paragraphs: The Persian king Ahasuerus (so in the Hebrew text and the King James Bible; the Russian Synodal translation calls him Artaxerxes) gives a feast lasting a hundred and eighty days, and then another lasting seven. On the seventh day, "when the heart of the king was merry with wine", he sends his chamberlains to bring Queen Vashti, "to shew the people and the princes her beauty". "But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment."

What happens next is the reason to reread this chapter. A wife's refusal is debated as an affair of state. The adviser Memucan fears not for the king but for what people will say: "this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes". The ruling is entered "among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered", and letters go out to every province "that every man should bear rule in his own house".

All three cards of the tail stand in that first chapter. The refusal to come and the fear of other people's talk are The Hanged Man. A marriage that falls apart in one evening is The Tower. A law for every house, written by one man, is The Emperor in his heavy version.

The end of the book answers its beginning. The last verse of chapter nine reads: "And the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book." A book whose first chapter declares the husband master of the house ends with a decree of the queen. Between those two verses lies the road of the couple 12-16-4: from the pause, through The Tower, to a law written by two.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 12 — The Hanged Man: "I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days"
paragraphs: Esther is an orphan, raised by her cousin Mordecai. She is taken into the palace by royal decree along with other young women, and before she meets the king she spends twelve months in purification: "six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours". The Hanged Man is the twelfth arcanum, and in this book the number twelve marks every wait. Twelve months before meeting the king. The lot for destruction is cast "in the twelfth year of king Ahasuerus" and falls "to the twelfth month". And in the twelfth month everything "was turned to the contrary".

"The king loved Esther above all the women" and set the royal crown on her head. But about the main thing Esther keeps silent: "Esther had not shewed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew it." She is already queen, yet she still obeys her guardian's word "like as when she was brought up with him". The voice of the parental home sounds louder in the marriage than the husband's voice, and the couple begins its life with a secret that one of them keeps at someone else's request.

The Talmud (tractate Megillah 13a) records a dispute about her names. Rabbi Yehuda holds that her real name was Hadassah, and that she was called Esther "because she concealed the truth about herself" (in the William Davidson translation on Sefaria): the Hebrew root s-t-r means "to hide".

The central scene of the entry is the law of the inner court. When Mordecai asks Esther to plead for her people, she answers: "whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death, except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live: but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days." Husband and wife live in one palace, and protocol stands between them. This is life in suspension, as with The Hanged Man: neither a break nor closeness, only waiting to be called.

For the couple 12-16-4 this is the common language. The two know perfectly well when it is better not to approach the other: before dinner, during the silence after work, while someone is "not in the mood". Each waits for the other to speak first. Important things are put off so as not to spoil the evening, and before anything difficult is said, the first thought is what the family will think. In the good version this is tact, rare attentiveness and a fine sense of the other: such a pair can feel each other at a distance and hardly ever wound with a careless word. In the heavy version it is those same thirty days in the inner court, when one does everything for the other, asks nothing for themselves and waits to be called.

Who is the "king" here and who waits in the court has nothing to do with gender. In one and the same couple the roles change from topic to topic: in a conversation about money one of them does the calling, in a conversation about parents the other.

The Hanged Man has a strong side too, and Esther shows it. When the king asks, "What wilt thou, queen Esther? and what is thy request? it shall be even given thee to the half of the kingdom", she asks for nothing and invites the king to a banquet instead. At the banquet he repeats the question, and again she defers: "let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I shall prepare for them, and I will do to morrow as the king hath said." It is a pause, but it has a date — tomorrow. **A pause with a date is the wisdom of choosing the moment. A pause without a date is thirty days of waiting to be called.**

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 16 — The Tower: a tree fifty cubits high
paragraphs: The Tower begins when the pause ends. Esther fasts for three days and goes to the king uncalled, "which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish". The push, as often happens with The Hanged Man, comes from outside. Mordecai sends word to her: "and who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

But in this book the tower itself is built quite literally, and another couple builds it. Haman, the great lord to whom everyone at the king's gate bows except Mordecai, leaves Esther's first banquet happy: the queen invited no one to the banquet with the king except him. At home he tells his wife Zeresh and his friends about his riches, his sons and his honours, and he ends like this: "Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate." His wife and friends reply: "Let a gallows be made of fifty cubits high."

The Russian Synodal translation says it outright: a tree, derevo. The Hebrew has ets, the same word as for any tree; the King James Bible renders it gallows. A tree for hanging, raised more than twenty metres high. **The Hanged Man's tree has grown to the height of a tower.** This is how 12 becomes 16: a grievance that hung in the air turns into a construction over one evening's conversation between husband and wife.

That night the king cannot sleep. He commands "the book of records" to be read to him and comes upon an old story: Mordecai once exposed a plot against the king. "What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this?" — "There is nothing done for him." The debt had hung in the book for years. The Russian Synodal translation reads "the Lord took sleep away from the king" (our translation) at this point: its translators followed the Greek version. In the Hebrew the king simply cannot sleep, and the name of God goes unmentioned here too.

In the morning Haman comes to ask for the hanging and himself devises the honour for "the man whom the king delighteth to honour", never doubting: "To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?" The honour goes to Mordecai, and Haman leads his horse through the city square. At home Zeresh tells her husband what everyone can already see: "If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him."

At the second banquet Esther finally speaks about the main thing: "For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish." The king asks: "Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?" — "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman." In one evening the king learns that his wife belongs to the people he signed away to destruction, and that his chief minister is the enemy. Two images collapse at once: of the wife he turns out not to have known, and of the adviser he trusted. The king rises "in his wrath" and goes out into the palace garden. Even The Emperor needs a pause between the blow and the verdict.

Haman dies on that very tree, and the same day the king gives his house to Esther: the fallen house passes to the one who waited. The book's great reversal is put like this: "in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, (though it was turned to the contrary...)". The Hebrew here is ve-nahafokh hu — "and it was overturned". The Hanged Man hangs upside down; The Tower turns over whatever was hanging.

For the couple 12-16-4, The Tower in the middle is not a prediction of disaster and not a promise of a break-up. It is the day when one of the two walks into the inner court uncalled and says what both had kept silent about. After such a day it is not the union that falls but the picture: an invented image of the partner, the comfortable version of "everything is fine with us", an order that rested on silence. This Tower has a harsh property worth knowing in advance: what is said on such a day is not forgotten. The words stay in memory like a decree in the book, and that leads straight to the main task.

sections.h2: Main task, 4 — The Emperor: a letter that cannot be revoked
paragraphs: Haman is dead, but his decree lives on. The letters of destruction went out in the king's name, sealed with the king's ring, and not even the king can revoke them. He tells Esther and Mordecai: "Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse." The most powerful man in his world cannot take back his own word. He can only allow a second letter, after which the first loses its force in practice.

The whole main task of the couple 12-16-4 is in this scene. For them The Emperor is not a throne but the laws of the house: "that's not how we do things", "I've said what I said", "we agreed once and for all". While such laws serve, they are a support: in Waite's list for The Emperor the first word is "stability". In the good version the four gives the couple what The Hanged Man lacks: clear agreements, savings for a rainy day, the certainty that the other will back them up. Trouble starts when a law once written by one of the two begins to get in the way of its own authors. The law of the inner court protected the king from strangers, and it ended up keeping his own wife from him for thirty days.

What has been said cannot be revoked, least of all after The Tower: the words of the day of truth stay in the book. But a second letter can be written — a new rule agreed aloud on top of the old one and sealed with a shared ring. Not "forget what I said back then" but "from now on, this is how we do it".

The heavy version of The Emperor in this book is not only despotism. King Ahasuerus barely rules at all. He hands his ring to whoever is nearby: first to Haman, to seal a decree against a whole people, then to Mordecai. After the decree of destruction, "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city Shushan was perplexed". The household learns the king's mood from a single line: "Then was the king's wrath pacified." In a couple this sounds familiar: "you decide", "do as you like", "I don't care" — and then a face on which no one can tell joy from anger. Deciding for both, and handing over the ring without asking what it will seal, are two sides of one trouble.

The book shows the strong version as well. Three times the king promises to grant Esther's request "even to the half of the kingdom". Not once does she take half the kingdom. She touches the top of the outstretched sceptre, stands before the king and asks not only about the letters but also speaks about herself: "how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred?" And then she writes: "Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority." The Russian Synodal translation has "with all insistence" (so vseyu nastoychivostyu, our translation). **A book whose first chapter declares that "every man should bear rule in his own house" ends with "the decree of Esther".** The Emperor's task in a couple is not to split the kingdom in half but to learn to sign the laws together.

And one last turn: irrevocability has not gone anywhere; it has changed its content. In chapter one, the banishment of the queen is written so that "it be not altered". In chapter nine, the days of Purim are fixed so that they "should not fail from among the Jews"; in the Russian text it is the same word as in chapter one. The steadiness that once banished now keeps joy. This is what a mature four looks like in a couple: the rules are still firm, but they are written by two and about what both hold dear.

sections.h2: Clues in Waite and Wen: the veil, the sceptre and truth unveiled
paragraphs: Of The Hanged Man, Waite says plainly that the main thing is not disclosed: "It is a card of profound significance, but all the significance is veiled." For a couple that enters its task through things left unsaid, nothing could be more exact. Nor for a heroine whose name is read as "she who hides".

Waite calls The Tower "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe". Unforeseen above all for the one who built: only the day before, Haman had left the banquet "joyful and with a glad heart". And in Wen's section on the reversed Tower there is a reading that might have been written about Ahasuerus: the jolt comes because the Seeker "relied on false impressions made by others". The king signed the decree after believing these words: "There is a certain people … neither keep they the king's laws."

Waite's Emperor holds a sceptre in the form of an ankh: "He has a form of the Crux ansata for his sceptre." Wen explains the signs of his power this way: "The scepter or crux ansata is his sovereignty; the orb is his dominion." In the Book of Esther, the king's power shows precisely in the sceptre: held out, it cancels the death sentence for entering uncalled. The queen "touched the top of the sceptre" — she touched his sovereignty, not his possessions. For a couple this is an exact image of the main task: to hold out the sceptre is to make an exception to one's own law.

Of The Star, which stands at the centre for half of these couples, Waite writes that "for the majority of prepared minds" its naked figure "will appear as the type of Truth unveiled", although he himself also sees in her the Great Mother of the Kabbalah. The entry of the tail is a veil. The centre of half such couples is truth unveiled.

sections.h2: The couple's centre: The Star that no one has alone
paragraphs: At the centre of the couple's matrix — the Atmosphere point, which shows what goes on between two people when no one is watching — the tail 12-16-4 has one of two cards: The Star (17) for 50.1% of couples or Justice (8) for 49.9%.

No birth date ever puts The Star at the centre of a personal matrix: a person's centre can only be 3–14, 16, 18, 20 or 22. Only the sum of two people produces it. A run of the site's engine through every date shows where it comes from: The Star stands at the centre for exactly those 12-16-4 couples in which one partner has the personal tail 3-7-22 with Justice (8) at the centre, and the other has the tail 9-9-18 with The Hermit (9) at the centre. 8 + 9 = 17.

Wen writes that The Star "appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower", and that "after the downfall of The Tower, The Star is an indication of a turn upward". Two of the four cards she names stand in this tail, and The Tower comes right before The Star in the deck: 16 and 17. Lisovskaya describes the atmosphere of The Star as a union in which people say straight out what they like and what they don't, and where, for once, the beautiful picture turns out to be true. For a couple that enters its task through silence, that is exactly what opens up after The Tower.

And the name? Most often the name Esther is derived from the Old Persian word for "star" (stāra; setāre in Persian to this day). In the same passage of tractate Megillah where Rabbi Yehuda reads the name as "she who hides", the Talmud gives the view of Rabbi Nehemya: "the nations of the world called her after Istahar, Venus". Both poles of the tail meet in one name: the veil of the entry and the star of the centre. **For half of the 12-16-4 couples, the atmosphere of the union bears the heroine's name.**

Justice, for the other half, comes from this book too. Wen stresses that this is "human-created justice, not divine justice". In the Book of Esther, where God is never named, judgement is done by people: the king, the queen, the scribes with the ring. The atmosphere of a couple with Justice at the centre rests on agreements, fairly shared duties and a sense that the rules are the same for both. Justice does not promise that everyone will get what they deserve; it speaks of how much it matters to these two that the law of the house is not written for one of them.

The couple's values — what the union exists for — are The Lovers for 87.2% of such couples and The Devil for 12.8%. The Lovers are a choice: "the king loved Esther above all the women". In Waite's list of divinatory meanings, The Hanged Man has the word "trials", and The Lovers have "trials overcome". That is what such couples are together for: a choice that went through the pause and did not break. In our reading, where the values sound through The Devil, the union is held by a strong attraction and a shared grip, and the task is to keep that grip from turning into a chain.

The tail 12-16-4 occurs in roughly one couple in 430 (0.233%), ranking 70th of the 97 couple tails. Every point of a couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, and this triple is built from only four combinations of personal tails. Which one a particular couple has can be seen from both partners' personal tails.
All four share one clue: neither partner has The Hanged Man or The Emperor in their personal tail. The pause and the law are born only between the two.

ul: **3-7-22 + 9-9-18 — half of couples (50%).** One partner's Empress and the other's Hermit give The Hanged Man: a generosity that gives everything away and a solitude that asks for nothing hang together in a pause. The Chariot and The Hermit give The Tower: one rushes ahead, the other withdraws. The Fool and The Moon give The Emperor: freedom and fog together demand a law. These couples always have The Star at the centre.

**6-8-20 + 6-8-20 — a quarter of couples (26%).** Both have the same personal tail. Two choices, The Lovers and The Lovers, give a pause: each waits for the other to choose. Two Justices give The Tower: two judges in one house. Two Judgements give The Emperor. By the engine's count, in every such couple each partner has The Emperor at the centre of their personal chart: the couple's main task is the very card that sits at the centre of each of them. Two kings in one palace learning to write one law. The couple's centre is Justice.

**18-6-15 + 21-10-16 — 16% of couples.** The Moon and The World give The Hanged Man, The Lovers and The Wheel of Fortune give The Tower, The Devil and The Tower give The Emperor. Only in this recipe does one of the two have The Tower personally: it stands on the karmic task of the partner with the tail 21-10-16. The couple's centre is Justice.

**3-13-10 + 9-3-21 — 7% of couples.** The Empress and The Hermit again give The Hanged Man, Death and The Empress give The Tower, The Wheel of Fortune and The World give The Emperor. The couple's centre is Justice.

paragraphs: Together, the first and last recipes account for 57% of couples: in more than half of them, the entry 12 is made of one partner's Empress and the other's Hermit.

The same order 12-16-4 also occurs as a personal tail, for 3,117 dates since 1900, and the site has a separate article about it. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and its conclusions do not carry over to a couple. No other couple tail is made of these three numbers: 12-16-4 is the only order.

sections.h2: A worked example: two people born on 07.08.1976
paragraphs: Take two people born on the same day, 7 August 1976 (07.08.1976). Their personal matrices are identical:

ul: karmic task — 7 + 8 + 5 = 20;
entry of the tail — 20 + 4 = 24 → 6, middle — 20 + 6 = 26 → 8.

paragraphs: Each has the personal tail 6-8-20, with The Emperor at the centre. Now add up the matching points of the two matrices:

The couple's centre is 4 + 4 = 8, Justice; the couple's values are 6, The Lovers. Here, as in any couple, the middle comes from adding the two middles, 8 + 8, not from the ends. That it also equals 12 + 4 is a property of the triple itself.

sections.h2: Two couples in one book: the weak and the strong version of the tail
paragraphs: In the Book of Esther the tail 12-16-4 is lived twice, by two couples.

Haman and Zeresh are its heavy version. Their common language is a grievance that hangs in the air: "all this availeth me nothing". Their joint evening project is a tree fifty cubits high. Their law is a decree written in someone else's name and sealed with someone else's ring. And they fall from what they built themselves. In real life the weak version of the tail starts far smaller and without any villainy: with a grievance that two people at the evening table do not talk through but keep building on.

Esther and the king are the strong version. Their pause has a date: "to morrow". The truth is spoken when it can be heard, and it is spoken about oneself. The Tower falls on the lie, not on the marriage. And they write the second letter together: the king gives the ring, the queen writes "with all authority".
Both couples have the same cards. **The difference lies in two things: what the pause is for and whose hand holds the pen.**

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the tail 12-16-4

ul: **Name the couple's own "inner court".** Every such couple has topics one partner does not enter uncalled: money, parents, the past, work. Until they are named, protocol rules them, not agreement.
**Have a sceptre.** A simple sign that lets either come in without an invitation — "is now a good time?" — and an agreement that this question gets an answer, not a brush-off.
**Give the pause a date.** Esther's "to morrow" is wisdom. "Some other time" is thirty days in the court.
**Do not build a tower out of a grievance.** Talk about whatever "gives no peace" while it is still a sentence, not a construction fifty cubits high.
**Go out into the garden, but come back.** On the day of truth, do not pass verdicts at the peak: the king first went out into the garden. But he came back.
**Write a second letter.** Instead of demanding "forget what I said", agree aloud on a new rule on top of the old one.
**Sign the law of the house together.** A decision that concerns both is made by both, and whoever made it explains why. Do not hand over the ring without asking what it will seal.

paragraphs: If the "law of the house" rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a task from the cards: it calls for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a call to a local emergency number.

ul: **Entry to the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** The couple's common language is the pause. These two know how not to come in uninvited, how to wait for the right hour and how to keep quiet about the main thing for the sake of peace. This shared wish is where the couple starts, and it is also what turns into resistance.

**Middle of the task — 16, The Tower.** The road from the pause to the task runs through a day of truth: what was kept back for a long time comes out, and the picture the house stood on collapses. Not the union — the picture.

**Main task — 4, The Emperor.** The law of the house. The lesson is not which of the two is in charge but how to write the rules together and rewrite the ones that have started to get in their own authors' way.

intro: The roles of the points follow Yuliana Lisovskaya's book on compatibility. The main point of a couple's tail is the third one, and the first two unfold it; Lisovskaya herself treats the middle as an "addition" to the main task, and the site reads it as the road from the entry to the task.

The first clue lies in the numbers themselves. The middle of a couple's tail is not worked out from its ends: it is the sum of the middles of two personal tails. But this triple has a coincidence built in: 12 + 4 = 16. A pause added to a law gives The Tower. Whatever waits a long time for its hour under strict rules comes out one day, and the Book of Esther shows exactly how that happens.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-16-4 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task written in three cards: the entry through The Hanged Man, the middle through The Tower, and The Emperor as the main task. The two begin with a pause and things left unsaid, pass through a day when what was hidden comes out, and learn to write the rules of their house together rather than by one person's decree.

faq.q: Does The Tower in the middle of a couple's tail mean a break-up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events or dates. The Tower here is the moment when the pause ends and the truth comes out. What collapses is the picture that rested on silence — an invented image of the partner or the comfortable version of "everything is fine with us" — not the union itself.

faq.q: How does the couple's tail 12-16-4 differ from the personal tail 12-16-4?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from a single date, and its points have their own roles. A couple's tail is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, and its points mean the entry to the task, the middle of the task and the couple's main task. The numbers are the same, but the calculation and the meaning are different, so personal conclusions are not carried over to the couple.

faq.q: Which personal tails make up the couple's tail 12-16-4?
faq.a: Only four combinations: 3-7-22 and 9-9-18 (half of couples), 6-8-20 for both (26%), 18-6-15 and 21-10-16 (16%), 3-13-10 and 9-3-21 (7%). To find out which applies, it is enough to look at both partners' personal tails.

faq.q: In a 12-16-4 couple, who is the "king" and who waits for an invitation?
faq.a: The cards do not assign roles by gender or character. Usually the roles change from topic to topic: on one question one partner does the calling, on another the other. It is more useful to notice in which topics the law of the inner court applies to the couple than to look for which of the two is The Emperor.

report: Haman is dead, but his decree lives on. Not even the king can take back his own word: "the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse." He can only allow a second letter — in the same name and with the same ring.

This is the couple's main task: for them The Emperor is not a throne but the laws of the house. "That's not how we do things", "I've said what I said", "we agreed once and for all". While such laws serve, they are a support. Trouble starts when a law once written by one of the two gets in the way of its own authors: the law of the inner court protected the king from strangers and kept his own wife from him for thirty days. The heavy version of the four is not only despotism. The king hands his ring to whoever is nearby without asking what it will seal, and the household learns his mood from a single line: "Then was the king's wrath pacified." In a couple it sounds like "whatever", "I don't care" — and a face on which no one can tell joy from anger.

The strong version: Esther does not take half the kingdom but writes "with all authority" together with Mordecai. **A book whose first chapter declares that "every man should bear rule in his own house" ends with "the decree of Esther".**

report.h3: What the pause is for, and whose hand holds the pen

report: The book lives this tail twice. Haman and Zeresh build a grievance up into a gallows and fall from what they built. Esther and the king give the pause a date, speak the truth when it can be heard and write the second letter together. Both couples have the same cards. **The difference lies in two things: what the pause is for and whose hand holds the pen.**
What changes the script for such a couple:

ul: name the couple's "inner court" — the topics one partner does not enter uncalled;
have a sceptre: "is now a good time?" — and an agreement that this question gets an answer;
give the pause a date: "to morrow", not "some other time";
talk about whatever "gives no peace" while it is still a sentence, not a construction;
on the day of truth, go out into the garden, but come back;
instead of demanding "forget what I said", write a new rule aloud on top of the old one.

report: If the law of the house rests on fear, threats or force, it is no longer a task from the cards: it calls for help from a psychologist, and in danger — a local emergency number or crisis line.

unit.title: The law of the inner court

captions.M: To want peace and wait to be called
captions.N: To get through the day when the hidden comes out
captions.D: To write the house laws together and rewrite old ones

unit.meaning: Your task is to give pauses a date, speak the truth in time and write your house laws together, not by one decree.
